opus-5.5.text:
I think it really comes down to the fact that you can't build great infrastructure in a vacuum. If you want to design the right chips, the right systems, the right software stack, you have to deeply understand the workloads that people will actually run on them. And the best way to understand a workload is to build it yourself.

At NVIDIA, our research team works on things like generative models, world models, physical AI, simulation. When we train these models ourselves, we feel the pain points directly. We see where the memory bandwidth becomes the bottleneck, where communication between GPUs slows things down, which operations are inefficient in our libraries, what kind of precision we can get away with. Those insights flow back to the architecture teams and the software teams, and they shape the next generation of hardware and tools.

If we only waited for customers to tell us what they need, we'd always be a step behind. Customers often tell you about today's problems. But research lets us look a few years ahead. Hardware design cycles are long, so a chip we start designing now might ship two or three years later. We need to anticipate where AI is going, and doing frontier research ourselves gives us that forward-looking view.

There's also a second reason, which is about the ecosystem. When we develop a model or a framework, like our work on Cosmos for world foundation models, we often release it openly. That helps the whole community build on top of our platform, and it shows what's possible. It lowers the barrier for developers, especially in areas like robotics and autonomous driving, where data and compute are hard to come by.

So for me, application research and infrastructure aren't separate things. They form a loop. We build applications to understand the infrastructure needs, we improve the infrastructure, and then that enables more ambitious applications. That loop is, I think, one of the reasons NVIDIA has been able to move as fast as the field itself.

r001.rationale: The response says NVIDIA must build and train applications itself to understand real workloads and their pain points, and connects those insights to what customers need from its hardware and software.

r002.rationale: It explains that hardware design takes years, so NVIDIA must use its own research to anticipate future AI needs before chips ship.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question I get a lot, and I think the answer comes down to one thing: you cannot build good infrastructure for something you don't deeply understand yourself.

NVIDIA's business is fundamentally about providing the computing platform for AI. GPUs, the networking, the software stack, CUDA, the libraries. But the thing about infrastructure is that it only becomes valuable when it serves real workloads. And the workloads in AI change very fast. Five years ago it was convolutional networks for images. Then transformers took over. Then diffusion models, then large language models, now video generation and physical AI, robotics, world models. Each of these shifts changes what the hardware and software need to do well. The memory access patterns are different, the communication patterns across thousands of GPUs are different, the bottlenecks are different.

If we only wait for customers to tell us what they need, we're always behind. By the time a customer has a problem at scale and reports it to us, that's already late in the cycle. So we need to be running at the frontier ourselves. When my team trains a large video foundation model, we hit all the problems first. We see where the data loading breaks, where the parallelism strategy doesn't scale, where inference latency becomes unacceptable. And then we can feed that back into the systems and software people, sometimes into the hardware roadmap itself.

The second reason is credibility and taste. When we build something and say to a developer, this is how you should do it, that recommendation is much stronger if we've actually done it ourselves. We've trained on tens of thousands of GPUs, we've dealt with the failure modes, we've felt the pain. That's very different from building tools in the abstract.

And honestly, the third reason is that for some areas, especially physical AI, there isn't yet a mature ecosystem to learn from. With language models, there are many companies pushing the frontier and the needs are relatively clear. With world models for robotics and autonomous driving, the field is still early. Someone has to go first, generate the data, build the simulation, train the models, discover what the infrastructure needs are. We think NVIDIA is well positioned to do that because we sit at the intersection of the compute, the simulation tools like Omniverse, and the research.

So it's not that we want to compete with our customers. It's that doing the application research is how we make sure the platform is actually good for what comes next, not just what exists today.

r001.rationale: The response says NVIDIA must run applications itself to encounter workload problems firsthand and feed those lessons into its systems, software, and hardware roadmap, helping it understand real application needs.

r002.rationale: The response says workloads change quickly and NVIDIA should prepare for what comes next, but it does not explain that long chip or computer-architecture design cycles require researching future needs in advance.

astra-6.text:
I think building good AI infrastructure requires understanding what people actually need to do with it. If we only look at individual components—how fast a chip runs or how well a library performs—we can miss the bottlenecks that show up when someone builds a complete application.

Doing application research ourselves gives us that firsthand experience. We work through the training process, the data pipeline, and inference, and we learn where the infrastructure helps and where it gets in the way. Those lessons can inform the hardware, the software, and how they work together.

Research also helps us anticipate future needs. The infrastructure we build takes time to develop, so we need some understanding of where AI applications are going. For me, application research creates that feedback loop: better infrastructure enables new research, and new research tells us how to build better infrastructure.

r001.rationale: It says doing application research provides firsthand experience with the training process, data pipeline, and inference, helping NVIDIA understand what people need and where infrastructure helps or hinders.

r002.rationale: It says infrastructure takes time to develop, so NVIDIA needs to understand where AI applications are going in advance.

sol-6.1.text:
To build good infrastructure, you need to understand the applications it will support. If we only wait for someone to tell us what they need, we may miss the underlying problem—or learn about it too late.

When we do application research ourselves, we experience the whole process: training models, debugging them, scaling them, and deploying them. That helps us understand where the bottlenecks are. Is it computation? Memory? Communication between GPUs? Or is the software making something unnecessarily difficult?

Those lessons help us design better hardware and software. And research gives us a view of what future applications might require, so we can start preparing the infrastructure before those needs become widespread. It creates a feedback loop: better infrastructure enables new research, and that research shows us how to improve the infrastructure.

r001.rationale: The candidate says doing application research themselves lets NVIDIA experience training, debugging, scaling, and deploying models, helping them understand bottlenecks and application needs.

r002.rationale: It says research reveals what future applications may require so infrastructure can be prepared early, but does not connect this to long chip or computer-architecture design cycles.
